EN.1.title: Climate Change & GHG Emissions
about: This indicator looks at how much the agri-food sector contributes to climate change and what it is doing about it. It covers three things: absolute emissions from farming and food processing, emissions relative to output, and carbon stored in agricultural soils. It also tracks mitigation, such as renewable fuel production. The indicator links the sector to Canada's Paris Agreement and 2050 net-zero commitments. It focuses on sector-wide results rather than individual producers or companies, and it does not cover adaptation to climate change or indirect (scope 3) emissions across the full value chain.
observations: Farm emissions have been flat for several years, but each dollar of output now carries less of them. Direct emissions from farming, including on-farm fuel use, were 69.75 Mt CO2e in 2024. That is 1.0% above 2023 and 0.8% above 2018, and the total has changed little since 2017 (Figure EN.1.1.1). Emissions remain about 37% higher than in 1990. Because Canada’s total emissions have declined while farm emissions have not, agriculture now accounts for 10.3% of the national total, up from 8.5% in 2010 (EN.1.1.3).

Methane and nitrous oxide account for almost all of it. Of the 56.4 Mt CO2e counted by gas in 2024 (which excludes on-farm fuel), methane was 31.2 Mt, nitrous oxide 21.8 Mt and carbon dioxide 3.4 Mt (EN.1.1.4). Most methane comes from enteric fermentation in cattle and from manure. Methane emissions have fallen by 20.7% since their 2005 peak, largely because the national cattle herd has shrunk since the mid-2000s.1 Canada has also joined the Global Methane Pledge, which aims to cut global methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030.2 Nitrous oxide emissions are up about 63% since 1990. Most of the increase comes from crop production, where emissions roughly doubled from 8.1 to 16.0 Mt CO2e as nitrogen fertilizer use grew with crop area and yields. These emissions are linked mainly to nitrogen inputs such as fertilizer and manure. They are the target of the federal goal to reduce fertilizer emissions by 30% below 2020 levels by 2030, and of 4R Nutrient Stewardship practices (right source, right rate, right time, right place; see EN.5).3 Carbon dioxide, mostly from liming and urea fertilizer, is small but has almost tripled since 1990.

Per dollar of output, Canadian agriculture has become considerably less emissions-intensive. Total agricultural emissions rose by about 14% between 2010 and 2024, but agricultural output grew faster. As a result, emissions per dollar of primary agriculture GDP fell by 26.9%, from 2.71 kg CO2e in 2010 to 1.98 kg in 2024.⁵ Food processing shows a different pattern. Its emissions intensity is about a tenth of the farm figure and has not improved, at 0.175 kg per dollar in 2010 and 0.180 in 2023, after peaking at 0.205 in 2013. Pesticide, fertilizer and other agricultural chemical manufacturing, a separate and energy-intensive industry, is far more emissions-intensive, and its intensity rose from 3.35 to 4.17 kg per dollar over the same period. Most of these emissions come from ammonia production for nitrogen fertilizer.

Food and beverage processing adds its own emissions on top of the farm figure. Direct emissions were 6.47 Mt in 2023, up 23.5% from 5.24 Mt in 2010 (EN.1.1.2). Miscellaneous food manufacturing is the largest source at 2.2 Mt, followed by meat processing at 1.2 Mt. Animal food manufacturing grew fastest, from 0.25 to 0.46 Mt, while seafood processing fell by more than a third.

For livestock products, life cycle assessments show emissions per unit of product falling. Beef emissions intensity declined from 12.6 kg CO2e per kg of live weight in 2014 to 10.4 kg in 2021, a 17.5% reduction.4 For chicken, emissions fell from 2.3 to 2.2 kg CO2e per kg of eviscerated chicken between 2016 and 2023.⁸ For milk, they were 0.97 kg CO2e per kg of fat- and protein-corrected milk in 2021, 9% lower than in 2011 (EN.1.1.5).⁹ Each study is updated only every few years, so these trends rest on a small number of data points.

Renewable fuel production rose by 37.0% between 2020 and 2025 (EN.1.3.1). Federal fuel policy has driven much of this growth. The Renewable Fuels Regulations set minimum renewable content in gasoline and diesel, and the Clean Fuel Regulations, in effect since 2023, require fuel suppliers to gradually lower the carbon intensity of their fuels.5 Much of this fuel is made from Canadian crops such as corn, wheat and canola, which links the sector to new markets for farm products. Plants also produce co-products such as distillers’ grains, which are used in livestock feed (see EN.6). Co-product output was steady at about 1.4 to 1.5 million tonnes over the same period. This measure tracks production, not how much renewable fuel the agri-food sector itself uses.

Longer-term soil carbon measures are steadier than the yearly sequestration estimates. Soil organic carbon on Canadian farmland has increased almost every year since the 1980s, with cumulative gains reaching 3,254 kg/ha by 2021. Over the same period, tillage erosion risk fell by 63.5% as conservation tillage and no-till were more widely adopted (see EN.2). These trends show that soils have been storing carbon over time, even though yearly estimates vary with the weather.
limitations: Carbon accounting for the sector remains incomplete. The National Inventory Report’s sequestration estimates exclude carbon sequestered on forage land that may offset enteric methane emissions, as well as carbon stored in on-farm trees and shrubs, such as shelterbelts and maple sugarbushes. In addition, agricultural carbon sequestration is not directly measured, soil carbon stocks are not reported, and biogenic carbon is not fully captured. The cropland figures presented here (EN.1.2.1) are therefore based on inventory estimates.

Certain accounting choices in the inventory affect how emissions are allocated. Perennial forage and silage crops are grouped with livestock rather than crops, which may shift emissions between the crop and animal figures in EN.1.1.5. Calculation methods also differ across sectors, so comparisons between farm and processing emissions should be made with caution, and sector detail is limited where proxy data are used. In addition, on-farm fuel combustion is reported together with forestry and fisheries in the inventory’s energy category.

The available data do not yet cover the full scope of the indicator. No data are available on the adoption of mitigation practices, on-farm renewable energy use, or progress toward national reduction targets. Renewable fuel production (EN.1.3.1) is the only mitigation measure, and it reflects production rather than use within the sector.

Coverage is also limited in some areas. The processing-sector series ends in 2023, and its emissions per dollar of GDP cover 10 of the 11 sub-sectors because GDP for tobacco is not published separately. Emissions intensity data for animal products come from life cycle assessments that are updated only every few years, so trends rest on a small number of data points. The Centre’s partners also note that definitions for measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) require further development
opportunities: Several aspects of this indicator’s purpose are not yet reflected in the available data, including the adoption of mitigation practices on farms, on-farm renewable energy use, and the sector’s progress toward national reduction targets. Some potential sources already exist. Statistics Canada’s Farm Management Survey and the Census of Agriculture collect information on practices such as tillage, nutrient management and manure handling, and on renewable energy systems on farms. Federal programs such as the On-Farm Climate Action Fund also report on the practices they support. Comparing sector emissions with the federal fertilizer emissions target and the agriculture projections in Canada’s 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan would show how the sector is tracking. Adding measures in these areas would bring the indicator closer to its intended scope.

Clearer measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) definitions would also help. Current accounting rules may not fully capture carbon stored in forage and silage systems, on-farm trees and shrubs, or soil carbon stocks. Further work on how these are defined and measured would give a more complete picture of the sector’s contribution to carbon sequestration.

EN.2.title: Soil Health
about: This indicator looks at the condition and long-term sustainability of Canada's agricultural soils, and at how farming practices affect their ability to support production, protect the environment, cycle nutrients, regulate water and store carbon. It treats soil as a living system: its structure, organic matter and biological activity decide how well it can sustain crops and livestock, keep water and air clean, and support human health.

To reflect this, the indicator pairs outcome measures, such as soil organic carbon and erosion risk, with practice measures, such as soil cover and crop rotations, because management choices are what shape soil condition over time. It fits the Environment block's focus on natural capital, resilience and sustainable land management, and it draws on established AAFC agri-environmental indicators as well as newer metrics. In the end, it should show whether soil condition and productivity are holding up, how much soils add to climate mitigation by storing carbon, and where erosion, degradation or fertility loss put farm output and water quality at risk.
observations: Soil cover on Canadian farmland reached 276.1 days per year in 2021, an increase of 8.2% since 1971 (EN.2.1.1). All of this gain occurred after 1981, when soil cover remained at about 255 days, the same as in 1971. The improvement largely reflects the decline of summerfallow and the wider adoption of reduced tillage and no-till, which leave crop residues on the soil surface.

The risk of soil erosion has declined substantially. Overall erosion risk fell by 57.4% between 1981 and 2021, from 12.75 to 5.43 (EN.2.2.1). Tillage erosion showed the largest improvement, falling by 63.6% (from 7.96 to 2.90) as conservation tillage and no-till practices were widely adopted. Wind erosion fell from 3.75 to 1.22, while water erosion improved the least, from 3.83 to 2.75. Nearly all of this progress occurred before 2011, when overall risk had already reached 5.63. Since then, water erosion risk has risen slightly, from 2.59 to 2.75.

Soil organic carbon has continued to increase. Cumulative carbon gains reached 3,254 kg/ha by 2021 (EN.2.3.2), and the relative organic carbon index rose from 0.763 to 0.791 (EN.2.3.4), with a slightly larger gain in the most recent decade than in the previous one. The annual gain increased from about 9 kg/ha in the 1980s to about 125 kg/ha since 2011, although it varies considerably from year to year, from 77 to 236 kg/ha during the 2010s (EN.2.3.1). The risk of soil organic carbon degradation fell from 2.47 in 1981 to 1.56 by 1991 and has remained near 1.5 since, on a scale where 1 is very low and 4 is high (EN.2.3.3). These gains are attributed mainly to reduced tillage, less summerfallow and higher crop yields, which return more residue to the soil.

These long-term trends provide context for the climate change indicator (EN.1). Soil carbon accumulates over decades, while cropland sequestration in any single year depends largely on weather. As a result, annual sequestration estimates do not necessarily reflect longer-term changes in soil carbon.

Farmland conversion is currently tracked and reported in only one province (EN.2.4.1). Alberta has monitored the fragmentation and conversion of agricultural land since 2011, recognizing that effective land use policy depends on reliable, long-term information. Between 2011 and 2025, the province lost about 82,600 ha of prime agricultural land (Classes 1 to 3), or 0.7% of the 12.3 million ha it had in 2011. Marginal land (Class 4) remained stable at 4.08 million ha, while non-arable pasture land (Classes 5 to 7) increased slightly, by about 18,400 ha. The rate of loss has slowed, from about 7,600 ha per year between 2019 and 2022 to about 3,800 ha per year between 2022 and 2025. Alberta’s experience shows how consistent, long-term monitoring can provide the evidence base for land use policy.
limitations: The indicator is intended to cover the physical, chemical and biological properties of soil. Current data mainly reflect physical and chemical aspects (erosion risk and soil organic carbon), along with soil cover, which reflects management practices, and all three are modelled rather than measured directly. The 2025 National Index notes that measures of compaction, biological diversity, drainage capacity, pH and salinity are missing, and that there is no composite soil health index. Practice measures such as crop rotation are also not yet included.

Soil biology is the largest gap. Partners note that biological datasets in regions such as Ontario and Atlantic Canada consist of one-time measurements. Results from tests such as permanganate oxidizable carbon (POXC), a measure of active carbon, are largely privately held and difficult to access, even though the testing is widely used.

Without a consolidated national dataset, access to provincial data varies considerably. No data were found for Saskatchewan. Quebec datasets are not publicly available and are covered by non-disclosure agreements with producers. Data from Atlantic Canada must be anonymized before release, and Alberta’s laboratory data are not centralized, so each private laboratory would need to be approached individually.

All national soil series end in 2021, as AAFC updates its soil indicators on a multi-year cycle. Water erosion is also calculated differently across regions (for example, Manitoba uses a 0 to 100 index, while Atlantic Canada uses other standard methods), which makes regional comparisons difficult.

Farmland conversion is tracked and reported only in Alberta, which has reported on it annually since 2011 (EN.2.4.1 covers 2011 to 2025). National Inventory Report data on the conversion of farmland to settlements are outdated, and Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Quebec do not publish comparable data.
opportunities: A composite soil health index combining physical, chemical and biological measures would provide a more complete picture than any single measure. Practice measures, such as crop rotation and residual soil nitrogen, would add context on what drives soil health outcomes.

Building reliable trend data will depend on data-sharing arrangements with provinces, including Quebec and Atlantic Canada, and with private laboratories in Alberta. It will also require an open, standardized set of biological or proxy indicators, such as POXC, to allow consistent comparisons over time and across regions. Alberta’s farmland conversion reporting could serve as a model for other provinces.

Two national initiatives could help address these gaps. The Government of Canada has committed to developing a National Agricultural Soil Health Strategy, in collaboration with the Soil Conservation Council of Canada, with a launch expected by December 2027.1,2 The strategy is expected to include support for soil data collection and closer work with the provinces and territories. Separately, the Growing Tomorrow initiative of the Arrell Food Institute at the University of Guelph is focusing its first year on healthy soils, with its first report expected in the first half of 2027.3 The initiative aims to identify where Canada is falling behind and where data collection should be prioritized. Both initiatives could help establish common methods, such as for POXC testing and water erosion, and support the development of a national soil health dataset.

EN.3.title: Water Stewardship
about: This indicator looks at how the agri-food sector uses water and how it affects water quality. It has two parts. Quality covers the condition of freshwater influenced by agriculture, including data from Health Canada’s Canadian Water Monitoring Program for Pesticides . Use covers the volume of water withdrawn for crop production, livestock and food processing. It reflects growing climate variability and rising expectations for responsible resource use. It does not measure water stress directly, climate adaptation outcomes or consumer water use.
observations: Agriculture can affect water quality through runoff of nutrients, sediment and pesticides from fields into nearby streams and rivers. Of the 31 river monitoring sites in agricultural areas, 38.71% were rated Excellent or Good for the 2022 to 2024 period, 41.94% Fair and 19.35% Marginal, and none were rated Poor (EN.3.1.1). These sites are part of a national network of 157 sites in southern Canada monitored by Environment and Climate Change Canada.

Health Canada’s Canadian Water Monitoring Program for Pesticides tests surface water in agricultural and other areas for a range of pest control products. Its results are published through the “Monitoring water for pesticides” dashboard (EN.3.1.2). The share of samples exceeding a reference value for at least one pest control product was 19.3% in 2022 (180 of 934 samples, 81 sites), 17.3% in 2023 (508 of 2,932 samples, 182 sites) and 16.3% in 2024 (639 of 3,913 samples, 279 sites). Because the number of samples and sites increased substantially as the program expanded, the apparent decline does not represent a like-for-like trend, and the network may also have shifted toward different sites. Health Canada notes that an exceedance does not necessarily indicate harm and may require further risk assessment.

Irrigation lets farmers grow higher-value and more water-intensive crops, such as potatoes, sugar beets, vegetables and forage, and it reduces exposure to dry years. Most of Canada’s irrigated land is in southern Alberta, where irrigation districts deliver water through shared canal and reservoir networks. National totals therefore largely reflect Prairie growing conditions.

Crop irrigation volumes peaked at 2.95 billion m³ in 2018, fell by 39.7% to 1.78 billion m³ in 2020, rose to 2.09 billion m³ in 2022 and declined to 1.89 billion m³ in 2024 (EN.3.2.1, EN.3.2.5). These changes largely follow growing-season weather in Alberta, where most of Canada’s irrigated land is located. Statistics Canada attributed the decline in 2020 mainly to rainier conditions and the increase in 2022 mainly to drier conditions. 1 In 2024, a wet spring in southern Alberta reduced early-season demand, although mountain snowpack was below average and conditions turned dry by mid-summer. 2,3 Changes in irrigated area and crop mix also contribute.

In contrast, irrigated area has grown steadily, from 605,907 ha in 2020 to 769,117 ha in 2024, an increase of 27.0% (EN.3.2.4). Over the same period, irrigation volume rose by only 6%, so water applied per hectare declined by about 16%, from roughly 2,940 m³ to 2,460 m³. At about 4,270 m³ per hectare, 2018 stands out as a high-use year. Improved irrigation efficiency may have contributed, as many producers have shifted to low-pressure pivot systems, but weather and crop mix also play a role. Tracking water use per hectare over time would provide a clearer picture. With climate variability expected to increase the frequency of dry years, irrigation is likely to remain an important tool for managing production risk.

Water use in both crop and animal production increased between 2019 and 2021, by 30.9% for crops and 21.1% for livestock (EN.3.2.2). Since 2009, livestock water use has increased by 43% and crop water use by 64%, although the series is reported only every second year. The 2021 drought on the Prairies likely accounts for part of the recent increase. For beef production specifically, irrigation of feed and forage accounts for approximately 99% of total water use, so changes in water use are driven largely by crop production rather than by cattle drinking water. Water-use intensity provides further context on production efficiency. Peer-reviewed life cycle assessment results show that the water-use intensity of Canadian beef remained relatively stable between 2014 and 2021, rising only from 654.7 to 657.3 L/kg live weight (EN.3.2.6).

In contrast, water intake by food and beverage manufacturers declined by 19.4%, from 406.1 million m³ in 2013 to 327.1 million m³ in 2021 (EN.3.2.3). The entire decline occurred in food manufacturing, where intake fell by 22.8% (from 367.0 to 283.4 million m³), while beverage and tobacco intake rose from 39.1 to 43.7 million m³. Without corresponding production data, it is not possible to determine whether this reflects improved efficiency or lower output.
limitations: Water stress, defined as water withdrawals relative to natural replenishment, is not measured at the national scale. Environment and Climate Change Canada discontinued this metric about 10 years ago. Without it, the indicator cannot show pressure on water supply or differences between regions.

Most metrics report total water use without linking it to production. As a result, changes in water use cannot be clearly attributed to efficiency gains, output changes or weather. For example, the decline in water intake by food manufacturers may reflect improved efficiency or lower output. Water use per unit of product is available only for beef (EN.3.2.6), and greenhouse water use is not tracked.

Water use is strongly influenced by weather, which makes underlying trends difficult to identify. Because irrigation is concentrated in southern Alberta, national irrigation totals largely reflect Prairie growing conditions. Combined with short series that are reported only every second year, this makes it difficult to separate the effects of weather from changes in irrigated area, crop mix or practices.

Several series have ended or have gaps. Statistics Canada has indicated that 2024 was the final release of the Agricultural Water Survey, as a result of their Budget 2025 spending reductions, so the irrigation series (EN.3.2.1, EN.3.2.4, EN.3.2.5) will not be updated. Water use in crop and animal production ends in 2021 and is reported every second year, and processing water use also ends in 2021, with irregular reporting years.

Water efficiency and water management practices, such as the type of irrigation system used, are not yet measured, even though the indicator is intended to show how efficiently water is used. The water quality series are also short: the river water quality data and the Canadian Water Monitoring Program for Pesticides data currently available both cover only 2022 to 2024.

Water stress, defined as water withdrawals relative to natural replenishment, is not measured at the national scale. Environment and Climate Change Canada discontinued this metric about 10 years ago. Without it, the indicator cannot show pressure on water supply or differences between regions.
Greenhouse water use is not tracked, and product-level water intensity is available only for beef (EN.3.2.6).

Water efficiency and water management practices are not yet measured, even though the indicator is intended to show how efficiently water is used. The water quality series are also short: the river water quality data and the Canadian Water Monitoring Program for Pesticides data currently available both cover only 2022 to 2024.

Several series end early or have gaps. Water use in crop and animal production ends in 2021 and is reported only every second year, and processing water use also ends in 2021, with irregular reporting years. Statistics Canada has indicated that 2024 was the final release of the Agricultural Water Survey, so the irrigation series (EN.3.2.1, EN.3.2.4, EN.3.2.5) will not be updated. In addition, because irrigation is concentrated in Alberta, national irrigation totals largely reflect Prairie weather conditions.
opportunities: Pairing water use with sector GDP or farm cash receipts would show water productivity, measured as dollars of output per cubic metre of water.

Product-level water intensity could be expanded beyond beef. Life cycle assessments for chicken and milk already report water use per kilogram of product and could be added. Greenhouse water use, which is not currently tracked, would also fill a gap.

With the discontinuation of Statistics Canada’s agricultural and industrial water surveys, a priority will be identifying alternative sources for agricultural and processing water use. These could include provincial irrigation and water licensing data, such as Alberta’s annual irrigation district reports, and work with Statistics Canada on how water use could be estimated through administrative data or modelling. Continued monitoring through the Canadian Water Monitoring Program for Pesticides will also be important for building useful trend data.
The largest gap, however, is the lack of a national water stress measure, and restoring one would add the most value to this indicator.

EN.4.title: Biodiversity & Agrobiodiversity
about: Biodiversity is difficult to measure directly, so this indicator uses measures such as wildlife habitat capacity on farmland, land-cover change and fish stock harvest levels as proxies to assess trends in condition of, and changes to habitats in agricultural and marine landscapes In the context of terrestrial agrobiodiversity, these measures provide insight into how well working farmland supports wildlife, ecosystem functions, and resilient food production. The aim is to better understand changes in the distribution of different land use types across our agricultural landscapes, and how those landscapes can support certain components of biodiversity, such as wildlife.
observations: Wildlife habitat capacity on agricultural land declined by 3.1% between 2000 and 2020, from 30.75 to 29.81 (EN.4.1.1). The index estimates how well agricultural land can support wildlife, based on the types of land cover present and their value as habitat for breeding and feeding. Most of the decline occurred between 2005 and 2015, when the index fell by about 0.07 to 0.08 points per year. Between 2015 and 2020, the rate of decline slowed to less than 0.01 points per year (EN.4.1.3). This may indicate that the decline is levelling off, although it reflects only one five-year period.

Changes in land cover help explain the decline. Between 2000 and 2020, native grassland and unimproved pasture, which provide the most valuable habitat, declined by 0.42 and 0.20 percentage points of agricultural land area, respectively. Coniferous and deciduous woodland declined by 1.75 and 1.25 points, and perennial cropland by 0.92 points. The largest gains were in regenerating woodland after harvest (+2.22) and annual cropland (+1.29), while built-up land, including settlements and roads, increased by 0.72 points (EN.4.3.1). Overall, these changes reflect a shift from natural and perennial cover toward annual crops and developed land.

Because native grassland and pasture are used largely for beef production, land associated with the beef industry accounts for most of the wildlife habitat capacity on Canada’s cropland and pastureland1. According to the National Beef Sustainability Assessment, reproductive habitat capacity on cropland and pastureland was 7.74 points in 2016, of which land associated with the beef cattle industry contributed 5.48 points (71%). By 2021, overall reproductive habitat capacity had decreased to 7.61 points because of land conversion, while the beef industry’s contribution increased to 5.63 points (74%). These results suggest that reproductive habitat on land used for beef production increased even as overall wildlife habitat declined. Note that these figures use different years and methods from the AAFC series above.

Fisheries, also part of the agri-food sector, show improvement over the past decade. In 2024, 96.5% of key fish stocks (191 of 198) were harvested at or below their removal references or other approved levels, up from 89.7% in 2011 (EN.4.1.2). Most of this gain occurred by 2013, and the share has remained between 94% and 99% each year since 2012. Because the list of key stocks has changed over time, comparisons between years should be made with caution
limitations: Habitat is a proxy for biodiversity, and the data do not reflect species-level trends, genetic diversity or long-term biodiversity tracking. The wildlife habitat capacity index focuses mainly on vertebrates and does not include pollinators or other invertebrates.
There is no measure of crop diversity or landscape heterogeneity, such as field size, buffers and other habitat features, and no composite or disaggregated view of biodiversity.

The available data are also dated and coarse. Habitat capacity is reported in five-year intervals up to 2020, land cover change covers 2000 to 2020, and the fish stock measure describes fisheries rather than farmland.

Farmland bird data from Birds Canada were assessed during the metrics review (January to June 2026).2 Although the data for the Prairies are detailed and cover a long period, they were considered too limited for this indicator because they do not cover other regions.

No metrics have yet been identified for agrobiodiversity, the diversity of crops, livestock and other organisms that support food production. The indicator therefore cannot show the diversity of crop varieties and livestock breeds in use, the conservation of genetic resources, or how well farmland supports services such as pollination and natural pest control.
opportunities: Biodiversity is difficult to measure, and data are the main challenge. Few datasets are collected at a national scale, repeated regularly and updated often enough to show change over time. Crop diversity, landscape heterogeneity, and pollinators and other invertebrates all shape the health of farmed landscapes, but the indicator does not yet reflect them. Datasets and metrics for these areas were explored during the review, and more work is needed to identify appropriate metrics and data before these measures, or a composite view of biodiversity, can be added.

While national data remain a challenge, provincial programs offer useful models. The Alberta Biodiversity Monitoring Institute (ABMI) monitors wildlife, habitat and human footprint across Alberta, and its approach could be considered by other provinces.⁵3

Agrobiodiversity is a priority gap, as no metrics have yet been identified. Potential starting points include crop diversity derived from Census of Agriculture land use data, national genetic resource collections for crops and livestock (such as those held by Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada), and the conservation status of livestock breeds reported to the FAO’s Domestic Animal Diversity Information System (DAD-IS). Further work would be needed to assess whether these sources are suitable for regular reporting.

EN.5.title: Crop Input Use & Management
about: This indicator looks at how fertilizers, pest control products and other crop inputs are used and how they are managed. It encompasses what is being used on Canadian farms and the adoption of best practices by farmers that improve environmental outcomes to soil, water and air, such as 4R nutrient stewardship (Right Source, Right Rate, Right Time, Right Place), nutrient use efficiency, variable rate application and soil testing. The aim is to improve productivity while reducing pressure on ecosystems. Because environmental outcomes are hard to measure at scale, this Indicator leverages proxy measures and practice adoption.
observations: Pesticide residues on food indicate whether pest control products are being used according to label directions, and therefore serve as an indicator of responsible use. Each year, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) tests domestic and imported foods for chemical residues and compares the results with the maximum residue limits (MRLs) set by Health Canada. Results for domestically produced fresh fruits and vegetables were selected because they reflect on-farm practices in Canada and are reported consistently over time. Compliance has remained high and stable, between 98.3% and 99.4% in each of the seven survey cycles since 2016–17 (EN.5.1.1). In the most recent cycle (2022–23), 9 of 1,289 samples exceeded an MRL.

Adoption of 4R Nutrient Stewardship (right source, right rate, right time, right place) is measured through Fertilizer Canada’s Fertilizer Use Survey, as the share of sampled hectares managed under 4R practices. Results are reported by crop and region as published, because combining them into a single national value would reduce accuracy. Only 2024 and 2025 use the same survey method, so comparisons are limited to these two years. Adoption increased in most crop and region combinations (EN.5.2.1). In Ontario, adoption on corn hectares nearly doubled, from 7.8% to 14.5%. In Western Canada, it rose from 26.2% to 35.3% for canola and from 29.9% to 36.9% for spring wheat, and in Manitoba from 33.8% to 40.9% for feed barley. The largest change was for malt barley in Manitoba, which rose from 8.4% to 42.6%. A change of this size over one year may partly reflect the small number of farms sampled for this crop and region, and it should be confirmed in future survey cycles. Adoption declined only for grain corn in Quebec, from 11.2% to 3.2%.

Variable rate fertilizer technology, which adjusts application rates within a field according to soil and yield variability, is used on a modest share of hectares, mostly between 7% and 20% across the crops and regions surveyed (EN.5.2.2). Trends differ between regions. In Western Canada, use has increased: for canola from 14.8% in 2019 to 19.5% in 2025, for spring wheat from 12.7% in 2016 to 17.4% in 2025, and for malt barley in Manitoba from 10.4% in 2022 to 19.4% in 2025. In Eastern Canada, use has declined: for corn in Ontario from 12.5% in [year] to 8.6% in 2025, for winter wheat in Ontario from 9.0% in 2015 to 2.1% in 2025, and for grain corn in Quebec from 10.3% in [year] to 7.7% in 2025. These regional differences may reflect differences in farm and field size, equipment and the nutrient management approaches commonly used for each crop, but the survey data do not identify the reasons.

Soil testing frequency depends on crop rotation, soil type and other factors (EN.5.2.3). In Ontario, for example, provincial guidance recommends testing each field at least once every three years.1 2In 2025, 82% of surveyed hectares in Manitoba and 70% in Western Canada were tested for nitrogen at least once every three years, compared with 47% in Ontario and 36% in Quebec. Annual testing is most common in Western Canada, where the share of hectares tested for Nnitrogen every year rose from 30% in 2019 to 45% in 2025, and it reaches 62% in Manitoba. In Ontario, most testing follows a three-year cycle, with only 3% of hectares tested every year. Testing for pH, phosphorus and potassium follows a similar pattern, although Ontario’s three-year testing is higher for these nutrients, at 65% of hectares.

Many producers use manure alongside commercial fertilizer as a source of nutrients, and good nutrient management accounts for both when matching nutrient supply to crop needs. The 4R principles also apply to manure, but the 4R adoption data reported here mainly reflect commercial fertilizer practices. Manure application methods help fill that gap. In 2021, liquid manure was applied to about 1.18 million ha, and on 58% of that area (682,433 ha) the manure was injected or incorporated into the soil (EN.5.2.4). These methods are generally considered good nutrient management practices because they help retain nutrients in the soil and reduce odour and nutrient losses. The remaining 499,637 ha received surface application, which generally increases the potential for nitrogen losses through ammonia volatilization. Data are available for only one year, so no trend can yet be assessed.

Nutrient use efficiency, the share of applied nutrients removed by harvested crops, varies from year to year, mainly with growing conditions (EN.5.2.5). Nitrogen use efficiency ranged from 62% to 81% between 2012 and 2024. It was lowest in 2021, when drought reduced yields and therefore the nitrogen removed by crops, and highest in 2022, and it has remained above 76% for the last three years. Nitrogen inputs held at about 5 million tonnes per year, while crop removal increased from 3.2 million tonnes in 2012 to 4.1 million tonnes in 2024. Phosphorus use efficiency ranged from 83% to 116% and has been above 100% since 2022. This means crops removed more phosphorus than was applied, drawing down soil phosphorus reserves, which over time could affect soil fertility if it continues.

New crop variety registrations are concentrated in oilseeds, at 58 to 214 per year, compared with 6 to 45 for each of the other major crop groups (EN.5.3.1). Soybeans account for most of these, with up to 181 registrations per year, and canola for 12 to 40. Oilseed registrations peaked at 214 in 2023 and were 62 in 2025. Registrations show that new varieties are being developed, but they do not indicate which traits, such as drought tolerance or disease resistance, are being targeted, or how widely the varieties are adopted by producers. As a result, the effect of new varieties on yields cannot yet be assessed (EC.5.1.1). For example, canola yields rose by about 32% between 2010 and 2025, from 1,900 to 2,507 kg/ha, while soybean yields remained at about 3,000 kg/ha despite soybeans having the most registrations. Weather has a strong influence on yields, as shown by the drop in canola yields to 1,593 kg/ha during the 2021 drought.
limitations: Practice adoption data are limited in time and coverage. Fertilizer Canada’s survey method for 4R adoption has changed over time, and only the two most recent years (2024 and 2025) use the same approach, so no trend can yet be established. Results are reported as the share of sampled hectares meeting all basic 4R criteria for nitrogen and phosphorus, for six crop and region combinations across four regions. They are presented as published, because combining them into a weighted national value could misrepresent actual adoption. As a result, the data are not national, and large single-year changes, such as the increase for malt barley in Manitoba, cannot be checked against earlier years. Sample sizes for some crop and region combinations may also be small. Variable rate technology and soil testing data likewise cover a limited set of crops and regions, and liquid manure application data are available for a single year.

Practice measures do not show environmental outcomes. The indicator tracks the adoption of practices and a national nutrient balance, but not the nutrient losses that affect soil, water and air, such as nitrogen leaching, nitrous oxide emissions or phosphorus runoff. A national nutrient balance can also mask regional differences, with surpluses in some areas and deficits in others.

The pest control measure has a narrow scope. Residue compliance covers domestically produced fresh fruits and vegetables only, and does not reflect field crops such as grains and oilseeds, which account for most cropland. It shows whether residues remain within limits, not how pest control decisions are made.

The link between inputs, productivity and environmental performance is not yet established and would likely require more in-depth study. New variety registrations do not track yields (EC.5.1.1), and publicly available national data do not link seeded area to specific varieties, so the effect of new varieties cannot be separated from changes in crop area or weather. The registration data also do not identify the traits that new varieties are intended to improve.
opportunities: Residue compliance shows the outcome of following label directions, but not how pest control decisions are made on the farm. A measure of integrated pest management (IPM) adoption would help fill that gap. IPM combines several methods, such as pest monitoring and cultural, biological and chemical controls, to manage pests effectively while limiting risks to people and the environment. Combined with residue results for food and water, IPM adoption would show how pest control decisions are made, whether products are used within their limits and whether residues are reaching the environment. Extending residue reporting to field crops would also improve coverage.

For nutrient management, extending the 4R, variable rate and soil testing series over more years, crops and regions would allow trends to be identified. The survey also reports other practices that could be added, such as the use of enhanced efficiency fertilizers, which reduce nitrogen losses. Repeating the liquid manure survey would make it possible to track change over time.

Outcome measures would complement practice adoption. AAFC’s agri-environmental indicators for residual soil nitrogen and the risk of water contamination by phosphorus estimate nutrient surpluses and potential losses by region, and could show whether improved practices are reducing environmental pressure.

For new varieties, data on the area seeded to each variety, available in some provinces through crop insurance programs, would show which varieties are being adopted. Information on the traits that new varieties target, such as drought tolerance or disease resistance, would help link innovation to productivity and resilience.

EN.6.title: Food Loss & Waste
about: This indicator looks at how much food is lost or wasted in the agri-food system, and how losses are prevented or put to other uses. The focus is on losses before the consumer: on the farm, in storage, processing and transport, and at retail. It covers two ideas, preventing loss and diverting what is lost, for example to animal feed, compost or upcycled products. It ties into national and global targets, including halving food loss by 2030. Consumer-level waste is out of scope, and there is no standard way yet to measure loss at every stage.
observations: Food loss and waste in Canada is considerable. The latest national study estimates that 21.2 million tonnes of food, about 46.5% of all food produced for Canada, is lost or wasted each year, including inedible parts such as bones and peels1. About 42% of this (8.8 million tonnes) is avoidable, meaning it was edible at some point, with a value of about $58 billion and about 25.7 million tonnes of CO2e in associated greenhouse gas emissions.

Within this indicator’s scope (before the consumer), avoidable food loss and waste was estimated at 6.67 million tonnes (EN.6.1.1). About two thirds of it, 4.39 million tonnes, is lost upstream in preharvest, storage and grading, and processing, with processing and manufacturing the largest single stage at 2.81 million. Distribution and retail add 2.28 million tonnes. The same source also estimates 0.67 million tonnes at restaurants, hotels and institutions and 1.48 million at households, which sit outside this indicator’s scope. The study reports that total food loss and waste fell by about 20% from its 2019 estimate, although differences in method between the two studies make the comparison uncertain.

Animal feed is also an important destination for Canadian grain. In 2025 the domestic feed industry used 80% of Canadian barley, 60% of corn and 30% of wheat production (EN.6.2.2). That grain becomes meat, milk, eggs and other animal products. While animal feed is an important destination for Canadian grain, livestock also make use of large quantities of co-products and by-products from other industries, which supports a circular bioeconomy and reduces waste2.

Oilseed crushing results in by-products that also go to feed. Canola meal production reached 6.79 million tonnes in 2025, up 32.7% from 2017, while soybean meal held between 1.2 and 1.6 million tonnes and came in at 1.22 million tonnes in 2024, its lowest level over this period (EN.6.2.3).⁴ Using the meal for livestock feed puts to work what is left after the oil is extracted. These volumes shouldn’t be compared directly with the food loss estimates, because the two are counted on different bases.
limitations: Canada has no regular, official national measure of food loss or food waste. Food loss (on farms, in storage, processing and transport) and food waste (at retail, in food service and in households) are not measured through any recurring national survey or statistical program. What exists comes from one-off studies that use different definitions, stages and methods 3,4. Results from different studies therefore can’t be compared or combined into a time series.

The Food Loss and waste figures presented in the National Index on Agri-Food Performance are based on the most recent available report from Second Harvest published in 20245. At this time, no information is available regarding a future update. The Reduce estimates (4.39 million tonnes before distribution, 2.28 million at distribution and retail) come from a report that relies on a 2019 baseline, while the 2025 National Index6 describes them as modelled on 2020 data.

Two Repurpose metrics, government waste-reduction funding and non-marketable wheat used for feed, were not updated in the 2025 cycle. This data may be a one-off, and future updates of the Food Waste Reduction Challenge, which feeds the Repurpose sub-indicator, remain uncertain.
With one snapshot there is no trend, so the data cannot yet show progress toward the national and global goal of halving food loss and waste by 2030.

Coverage is narrower than the scope. The indicator is meant to cover avoidable and unavoidable (inedible) loss, and diversion to animal feed, compost, upcycled products, biofuels and anaerobic digesters. The data cover avoidable loss only, diversion only through animal feed (grain shares and oilseed meal), and nothing on prevention initiatives. Data on co-products and by-products fed to livestock are limited. Partners note that cattle consume substantial volumes of these materials, but the amounts are hard to measure because supply varies with the output of the industries that produce them. Better data on these volumes would show more fully how much material the livestock sector keeps in use.

Comparisons with global data are unreliable. FAO Food Systems Dashboard figures for cereal, pulse, vegetable and fruit loss put Canada above the world average, which partners find counterintuitive and want investigated.
opportunities: The most significant gap is the lack of national data. A recurring national measurement of food loss and food waste would provide the indicator with a reliable baseline and trend. Ideally, this measurement would be led or coordinated by Statistics Canada and apply a consistent method across all stages of the supply chain. Aligning it with international methods, such as the Food Loss and Waste Accounting and Reporting Standard and the FAO Food Loss Index and UNEP Food Waste Index used to report on SDG Target 12.3, 7 would also allow more reliable comparisons with other countries. Ongoing work toward a national voluntary standard for food loss and waste, supported by Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, could provide common definitions to support this measurement.8

Until national data are available, regular updates of the Reduce estimates and Repurpose metrics would help show whether food loss and waste is declining. The current picture focuses on avoidable loss and a single diversion route. Including unavoidable loss, and other diversion routes such as composting, anaerobic digestion and upcycled products, would show more fully how much material is kept in use. Improved tracking of the co-products and by-products used in livestock feed would also strengthen the indicator. Prevention initiatives, and the policies and funding programs that support them, are also worth capturing, as they show what is driving change.

Comparisons with global figures also require further examination. A closer review of the methodology behind the FAO Food Systems Dashboard would show whether Canadian and global figures are sufficiently aligned to be compared with confidence.

EN.7.title: Packaging & Waste
about: This indicator looks at how packaging and plastic waste is generated, managed and reduced across the agri-food system, using the reduce, reuse and recycle framework. It covers on-farm plastics such as pesticide containers and grain bags, as well as packaging used in processing and retail. It tracks diversion, recycling and uptake of circular practices, in support of national commitments on plastic waste. It does not yet measure reuse at scale or capture every type of packaging.
observations: Collection of small pesticide and fertilizer containers (up to 23 L) has improved, although not in a straight line. Proper collection prevents empty containers from being burned or buried on farms, which can release pesticide residues and other pollutants into soil, air and water. Cleanfarms1 runs a national program, through agri-retailers and municipalities, that collects empty, rinsed containers from farms and recycles them into products such as agricultural drainage tile. The collection rate compares the amount collected with the amount sold into the market, as a three-year moving average updated each year. It was 66% in 2013, remained at about 61% to 62% from 2014 to 2017, and has increased since 2018, reaching 88% in 2025, with a single decline in 2022, from 77% to 73% (EN.7.1.3). Cleanfarms describes this rate as one of the highest in the world for crop input containers. The weight collected rose by 53%, from 1.63 kilotonnes in 2011 to 2.50 kilotonnes in 2025 (EN.7.1.1), including a 13% increase from 2024 to 2025. Since the program began, about 61 million kg of small containers have been collected.

Collection of larger containers and other farm plastics shows a similar trend, although these are not yet included in this indicator. In 2025, Cleanfarms collected 109,000 bulk totes and drums (24 to 1,000 L), an increase of 13% from 2024, with a three-year average collection rate of 63%. In Saskatchewan, where a provincially regulated program collects used grain bags, 1.65 million kg were collected in 2025.23

Results for plastics more broadly are less positive (EN.7.1.2).[3] This series covers all plastics diverted from disposal in Canada, not only agri-food packaging. Residential plastics diversion declined from 230,777 tonnes in 2018 to 198,756 tonnes in 2022, then recovered to 235,198 tonnes in 2024, about 1.9% above the 2018 level. Non-residential diversion, which includes industrial, commercial and institutional sources such as food processing and retail, fell from 97,813 tonnes in 2018 to 66,883 tonnes in 2024, a decline of 31.6%. This is the only measure in the packaging and waste indicator that shows a clear decline.
limitations: Cleanfarms now reports small container collection by weight (kilograms) rather than by number of containers, and the container series in this indicator (EN.7.1.1) uses this measure. The collection rate (EN.7.1.3) is a three-year moving average updated each year, which smooths year-to-year changes, so recent shifts appear only gradually.

The collection rate measures collection rather than recycling. Cleanfarms reports what collected containers are made into, but, except for bulk containers, not how much material is actually recycled after processing. The share of the total agricultural container market covered by the program is also not published. In addition, bulk containers, grain bags and other farm plastics collected by Cleanfarms are not yet included in the indicator.

The reduce and reuse dimensions are not measured. No data were found for the Reuse sub-indicator, even though it was identified in 2023, and there is no measure of the amount of packaging generated, which would be needed to track reduction. The three metrics in this indicator therefore reflect collection and diversion only.

Collection volumes differ by region, partly because provincial rules differ. Some Cleanfarms programs are regulated or fall under extended producer responsibility (EPR) requirements in certain provinces, while others are voluntary or operate as pilots. National totals and trends therefore combine results from different regulatory frameworks.

Coverage is narrower than the indicator’s intended scope. The plastics diversion series (EN.7.1.2) covers all plastics diverted in Canada, not only agri-food packaging, so the sector’s contribution cannot be separated. The series begins in 2018 and does not explain the causes of change, such as the decline in non-residential diversion. Packaging used in food processing and retail is not measured.
opportunities: Agri-specific plastics are the most ready addition. Cleanfarms already reports collection of bulk pesticide and fertilizer containers, grain bags and twine, including a collection rate for bulk containers and a regulated grain bag program in Saskatchewan. Adding these series would cover on-farm plastics beyond small containers. Showing collection results next to each province’s extended producer responsibility (EPR) rules would help explain why recovery differs across the country.

The indicator could also look beyond collection. Data on how much collected material is actually recycled would show whether collection translates into recovery. A measure of packaging used in processing and retail would extend the indicator further along the supply chain, and provincial EPR programs for packaging may become a source for it as they report more data.

Reuse is the clearest gap, since it still has no metric at all. Measuring it would likely take dedicated discussions with researchers and small and medium-sized businesses working in this space, possibly through a separate project to explore how reuse could be tracked.
FOOD INTEGRITY
notes: Cleanfarms is a non-profit stewardship organization whose members include crop input and animal health companies. It collects agricultural plastics and products across Canada, including empty pesticide and fertilizer containers, and publishes annual results by program and province.

FI.1.title: Safe Food
about: The Safe Food indicator assesses the performance of Canada’s food safety system, focusing on the outcomes of regulatory oversight, population health outcomes, compliance, and system response to food safety risks across the agri-food system.

The indicator measures system-level food safety safeguards that underpin trust in Canadian food and support access to domestic and international markets. It assesses the overall safety of Canada’s food system through regulatory compliance, investigations, recalls, chemical-residue monitoring and foodborne illness. New metrics have been added to provide more accurate and comprehensive information on prevention, detection and response, while recognizing that no single measure can determine whether the food supply is becoming safer.
observations: Canada continues to record high regulatory compliance. The proportion of tested imported and domestic food products meeting federal requirements increased from 97.6% in 2022–23 to 98.6% in 2024–25. The percentage of federally registered food establishments that corrected identified issues following inspection also rose from 75.4% to 85.8%, reaching the CFIA target of at least 85%.

Public confidence has also improved. The percentage of Canadians who agreed that the CFIA helps ensure food sold in Canada is safe increased from 71.5% in 2022–23 to 82% in 2024–25. This new metric responds to an opportunity identified in 2025 by providing information on public perceptions of Canada’s food-safety oversight.

Food-safety investigations increased from 2,529 in 2021–22 to 3,934 in 2025–26, while recalls rose from 196 in 2024 to 271 in 2025. These increases may reflect changes in food-safety risks, but they may also result from stronger surveillance, reporting, or regulatory activity. Even though, Investigation and recall totals alone do not demonstrate that food became less safe.

The proportion of higher-risk recalls initiated before an adverse effect was reported declined from 92.1% in 2023–24 to 71.9% in 2024–25. This decline warrants attention because the measure reflects the system’s ability to identify and remove higher-risk products before illnesses or injuries are reported.

Residue monitoring results continue to demonstrate strong performance, with available compliance rates generally above 93%. In 2020–21, pesticide-residue compliance was 99.2% for domestic fresh fruits and vegetables and 93.8% for imported products.

The addition of foodborne illness outbreak data to the Index provides further information on food safety outcomes. In 2024, the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) coordinated investigations of 10 outbreaks involving 286 reported cases, compared with six outbreaks and 693 cases in 2023. Salmonella accounted for four outbreaks and 122 cases in 2024. Although the number of outbreaks increased, associated cases declined by approximately 59%. Annual results can be influenced by a small number of large outbreaks and should be interpreted cautiously.
limitations: Assessing Canada’s food-safety performance remains challenging because relevant results are dispersed across several departmental reports, surveillance studies and recall databases that use different measures and coverage. Recall totals must also be interpreted carefully: one incident can generate numerous product recalls. Canada’s surveillance system depends on information shared among federal, provincial, territorial and regional authorities, which can affect the completeness and timeliness of national reporting. Additional limitations include inspection coverage gaps, uneven traceability across complex supply chains, risks associated with imported foods and food fraud, and limited publicly consolidated information connecting inspections, recalls, illnesses and corrective actions over time.
opportunities: Canada already has several initiatives supporting stronger food traceability. The Safe Food for Canadians Act Regulations require most food businesses to maintain one-step-back and one-step-forward records. CFIA also manages the national Livestock Traceability Program, has explored boat-to-plate traceability for seafood and completed a blockchain pilot for supply-chain information sharing1. Its current digital modernization agenda includes updated data and analytics strategies and improved digital-service platforms. Together, these initiatives provide a strong foundation and an opportunity to develop an interoperable, end-to-end digital traceability system that enables faster investigations, more targeted recalls and improved detection of food fraud.
notes: CFIA completed a two-year initiative examining the practical application of blockchain for information sharing, supply-chain management and traceability. https://inspection.canada.ca/en/about-cfia/acts-and-regulations/forward-regulatory-plan/targeted-regulatory-review

FI.2.title: Nutrition Information
about: The Nutrition Information indicator assesses Canada’s approach to providing transparent, standardized, and reliable nutrition information to consumers. It focuses on the availability, accessibility, and clarity of nutrition information provided through regulatory frameworks, disclosure requirements, labeling and public guidance and advice that support informed food choices and healthier diets at the population level. The indicator captures key areas related to nutrition labelling, front-of-package labelling, nutrition information availability, and consumer transparency . It evaluates the extent to which consumers have access to consistent and understandable nutrition information across the food system.

While the indicator aligns strongly with the Food Integrity Block through its focus on transparency and consumer access to information, it does not directly measure nutrition or health outcomes, dietary behaviours, or the overall nutritional quality of diets.

New metrics have been added to provide a more accurate and comprehensive assessment. The previous Indicator focused mainly on the existence of nutrition-labelling and fortification requirements. The expanded metrics include use of Health Canada’s dietary guidance, nutrient-content and disease-risk-reduction claims, implementation of front-of-package labelling, and food misrepresentation. These additions broaden the Indicator from documenting regulations to considering how nutrition information is communicated, used, and accurately represented.
observations: Canada’s Food Guide remains the foundation of national dietary guidance. It was last updated in 2019, replacing the 2007 version. Health Canada’s 2025 evidence review1 concluded that the current dietary guidance remains scientifically relevant, while identifying emerging evidence that may inform future updates.

Nutrition information can be mandatory, including the Nutrition Facts table, ingredient list and allergen declarations, or voluntary, including nutrient-content claims such as “source of calcium” or “low in fat.” Disease-risk-reduction claims may also be used when foods meet prescribed conditions. Permitted claims address relationships between diet and health outcomes such as hypertension, osteoporosis, heart disease, cancer, and dental caries.

The most significant regulatory change since the 2025 Index is the implementation of front-of-package nutrition labelling. As of January 1, 2026, most prepackaged foods that meet or exceed prescribed thresholds for saturated fat, sugars, or sodium must display a front-of-package “high in” symbol, subject to regulated exemptions. Products imported, manufactured in Canada, or packaged at retail before that date may continue to be sold.2 This requirement responds directly to an opportunity identified in the 2025 Update Index Report and provides consumers with more visible information about nutrients of public-health concern.

The percentage of Canadians who reported s using Health Canada’s dietary guidance was 44.3% from 2022–23 through 2024–25, below the federal target of at least 50%. However, these results rely on Canadian Community Health Survey data last made available in 2021–22 and do not represent newly measured annual values.3

Canada also requires specified foods to be fortified with particular nutrients. Examples include iodine in table salt, vitamin D in milk and margarine, and B vitamins, iron, and folic acid in white flour.

The addition of food-misrepresentation data recognizes that nutrition information must be accurate and trustworthy. In targeted 2022–23 testing, satisfactory results ranged from 62% for other expensive oils and 68% for grated hard cheese to 90% for fruit juice and 98% for meat.
limitations: Assessing nutrition information in Canada remains challenging because several measures track the existence of regulatory requirements rather than their implementation or effectiveness. Public data are limited on the number of products requiring front-of-package symbols, compliance rates, nutrient-content claims and changes in product formulation. The indicator also does not assess whether consumers understand nutrition information or whether it changes purchasing and dietary behaviour. Health Canada’s repeated 44.3% result for 2022–23 through 2024–25 relies on Canadian Community Health Survey data last available in 2021–22 and therefore cannot demonstrate annual change. The recent introduction of mandatory front-of-package labelling also means that its effects cannot yet be evaluated reliably.
opportunities: Canada’s implementation of front-of-package labelling and new supplemented-food requirements creates an important opportunity to improve both nutrition information and its measurement. These initiatives could support systematic monitoring of label compliance, consumer awareness and understanding, product reformulation and changes in consumer purchasing behaviour. Combined with Canada’s Food Guide, consumer-education resources and ongoing monitoring of food advertising to children theyprovide a foundation for assessing whether nutrition policies improve access to clear information and support healthier choices. Establishing a national baseline and publishing regular results would allow Canada to move beyond measuring the existence of requirements toward evaluating their implementation, reach and effectiveness.

FI.3.title: Antimicrobial Stewardship
about: The Antimicrobial Stewardship indicator assesses Canada’s approach to promoting the responsible, prudent, and sustainable use of antimicrobials across the agri-food system. It focuses on the policies, practices, monitoring systems, and stewardship measures implemented to reduce antimicrobial resistance risks while supporting animal health, food system integrity, and public health protection.

In Canada, sales of antimicrobials for farmed and domestic animals are tracked through national surveillance systems, including the Veterinary Antimicrobial Sales Reporting system and the Canadian Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System (CARSS). CARSS also monitors antimicrobial use and resistance trends across human and animal health. Together, these datasets provide an evidence base for assessing stewardship progress and identifying risks to public health and the agri-food system from growing antimicrobial resistance.

Updated species-specific sales and resistance metrics provide a more accurate and comprehensive assessment than total sales alone. They also strengthen alignment with the "One Health” approach, which recognizes the connections among human, animal, plant, and environmental health1.
observations: Total veterinary antimicrobial sales declined from 1,064.3 tonnes in 2020 to 917.17 tonnes in 2024, a reduction of approximately 13.8%. Sales in 2024 were also 6.1% lower than the 976.8 metric tonnes reported in 2023. This sustained decline is a positive development, although sales volume alone cannot determine whether antimicrobials were used appropriately or explain the factors driving the change.

Species-specific results present a mixed picture. Between 2023 and 2024, biomass-adjusted sales of medically important antimicrobials increased for pigs from 134 to 139.5 milligrams per kilogram of biomass. Sales declined for cattle from 66 to 56.5 mg/kg and for poultry from 68 to 48.1 mg/kg over the same period. These decreases suggest continued progress in some production sectors.

In contrast to the decline reported in the 2025 Index, aquaculture sales increased sharply from 58 mg/kg in 2023 to 221.9 mg/kg in 2024. This increase should be interpreted cautiously because changes in animal biomass, disease conditions, production cycles, and the timing or attribution of sales can produce substantial annual variation. Additional information is needed to determine whether the result represents a sustained change.

Antimicrobial resistance remains a significant concern for the Canadian agri-food industry. Between 2018 and 2022, CARSS identified upward trends for several priority infections, including community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) bloodstream infections, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus, carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales, and resistant Salmonella infections. Healthcare-associated MRSA bloodstream infections, Clostridioides difficile infections, and drug-resistant tuberculosis remained stable.2

The addition of resistance trends strengthens the Indicator by recognizing that stewardship involves both responsible use and the preservation of treatment effectiveness. However, the reported resistance trends relate mainly to human infections and cannot be attributed directly to antimicrobial use in agriculture.
limitations: Current data are largely based on sales information, which provides a useful proxy but does not show how antimicrobials are administered on farms or whether they are used for treatment, disease prevention, or other purposes. Biomass adjustment improves comparison but does not fully account for production systems, disease pressure, animal lifespans, or treatment intensity.

Coverage across the One Health spectrum remains uneven. The resistance component primarily describes human infections and is not directly linked to animal-use results. Reporting periods also differ, with sales data extending to 2024 and most resistance trends ending in 2022. Environmental surveillance and nationally representative farm-level data remain limited.
opportunities: Future reporting could integrate sales data with farm-level use, prescribing purposes, animal-health outcomes, and resistance findings from animals, food, people, and environmental sources. Results could also be presented by antimicrobial class, administration route, species, production stage, and region.

Canada’s 2023–2027 Pan-Canadian Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance provides an opportunity to strengthen standardized One Health surveillance and integrate antimicrobial-use and resistance data across sectors.3 Developing linked, longitudinal datasets would support clearer assessment of stewardship progress, improve international comparability, and reinforce the credibility of Canada’s antimicrobial stewardship efforts.
